title: Your secret weapon: break any sentence into carriage, engine and modifiers
summary: Every long sentence is a が carriage and an engine, with everything else telling you more about one of them.

blocks.text: A very long Japanese sentence is usually less complicated than it looks. Every logical clause has just two core parts: the **が main carriage** (visible or zero) and the **engine**. They are not just part of the sentence: **they are the sentence**. Everything else only gives more information about one of them.

Lesson 46 said modifiers go before the noun. The full rule is wider: **anything that modifies anything goes before it**. That includes the engine. In an other-move sentence, the nouns marked by **を, に, で and へ** are all modifiers of the verb: each tells you more about the action. (の is different: it links one noun to another noun.)

blocks.en: (I) ran in the park. (ran: where? in the park)

blocks.text: The carriage can have a describer too
When the carriage needs a describer, the describer is in front of it and must be visible.

blocks.jp: 本を読んでいる女の子は私の妹だ。
blocks.en: The girl who is reading a book is my little sister.

blocks.text: Take the sentence below. Its core is only (私が) あげた, "I gave". Everything else answers a question about it. First the core on its own, then the full train:
Everything else hangs off the core, like a train growing carriage by carriage.

blocks.jp: （私が）母が焼いたケーキを眼鏡をかけた女の子にあげた。
blocks.en: (I) gave the cake my mother baked to the girl wearing glasses.

blocks.text: Take the sentence below. Its core is only (私が) あげた, "I gave". Everything else answers a question about it.

Peel the sentence like this: find the final engine, find its carriage, then ask each other piece "what are you telling me more about?" Pieces ending in an engine in front of a noun are simply clauses describing that noun.

A sentence can hold two complete clauses. Both have a carriage, and the second one shares the first one's zero carriage. English does the same: "I went to the shop and bought bread" does not say "I" twice. The more clauses you can recognize, the more manageable long sentences become.

blocks.jp: 店に行ってパンを買った。
blocks.en: (I) went to the shop and bought bread.

blocks.text: The same chain works inside a single word. 外国人 is 外 (outside) → 国 (country) → 人 (person): a person of a country that is outside.

items: Every logical clause is a **carriage + engine**; the rest modifies one of the two.
**を, に, で, へ** nouns modify the verb; **の** links two nouns.
Anything that modifies something stands **before** it.
To read a long sentence: find the engine, find the carriage, then attach each piece.

questions.instruction: What are the two core parts of every logical clause?
questions.note: The carriage and the engine are the sentence; everything else modifies one of them.

questions.instruction: Which particle links one noun to another instead of modifying the verb?
questions.note: の joins two nouns; を, に, で and へ nouns modify the verb.

questions.instruction: What is the core of this sentence?
questions.prompt: （私が）友達が作ったカレーを食べた。
questions.note: Carriage plus engine: (I) ate. The rest answers questions about it.
questions.en: I ate the curry my friend made.

questions.instruction: What does 駅で tell us more about?
questions.prompt: 昨日、駅で友達に会った。
questions.note: A で noun modifies the verb: where the meeting happened.
questions.en: (I) met a friend at the station yesterday.

questions.instruction: What does the clause 青いシャツを着た describe?
questions.prompt: 青いシャツを着た男の人が来た。
questions.note: A clause that ends in a verb in front of a noun describes that noun.
questions.en: The man wearing a blue shirt came.

questions.instruction: True or false?
questions.prompt: 毎朝、パンを食べる。 パンを modifies the engine 食べる.
questions.note: A を noun tells you more about the verb: eat what?

questions.instruction: True or false?
questions.prompt: 日本の友達 In this phrase の links two nouns.
questions.note: の links 日本 to 友達.

questions.instruction: Which question does 公園で answer?
questions.note: で marks where the action happened and modifies 遊んだ.
questions.en: My younger brother played in the park.

questions.instruction: How many logical clauses (engines) are there?
questions.prompt: 駅に行ってコーヒーを飲んだ。
questions.note: 行って and 飲んだ are two engines.
questions.en: (I) went to the station and drank coffee.

questions.instruction: What is the carriage of 買った?
questions.prompt: 店に入って、水を買った。
options: A zero (私が), shared with the first clause
questions.note: Both clauses share one zero carriage, as English does with "I went in and bought".
questions.en: (I) went into the shop and bought water.

questions.instruction: What does 妹に answer?
questions.prompt: （私が）先生が書いた手紙を妹にあげた。
questions.note: に tells more about the engine あげた: to whom.
questions.en: I gave my little sister the letter the teacher wrote.

questions.instruction: What does the clause 先生が書いた describe?
questions.prompt: （私が）先生が書いた手紙を妹にあげた。
questions.note: It ends in a verb and stands before the noun 手紙.
questions.en: I gave my little sister the letter the teacher wrote.

questions.instruction: Tap the engine
questions.note: The engine is the core; 大きい describes かばん.

questions.instruction: Tap the word that 赤い describes directly
questions.note: A describer goes straight before what it describes.
questions.en: The woman wearing red clothes came.

questions.instruction: Tap the noun that 姉が焼いた describes
questions.note: A clause ending in a verb describes the noun after it.
questions.en: The bread my older sister baked is delicious.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: I read the letter my younger brother wrote.
questions.note: 弟が書いた is a clause that describes 手紙.
questions.en: I read the letter my younger brother wrote.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: I talked to the friend I met at the station.
questions.note: 駅で会った describes 友達; 話した is the engine.
questions.en: I talked to the friend I met at the station.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: I went to school and studied.
questions.note: Two clauses share one zero carriage.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: The movie I watched yesterday was interesting.
questions.note: 昨日見た describes 映画; the engine closes the sentence.
questions.en: The movie I watched yesterday was interesting.

questions.instruction: What does バスで tell us more about?
questions.prompt: 弟は毎日バスで学校に行く。
questions.note: で modifies the engine: how did he go?
questions.en: My younger brother goes to school by bus every day.

questions.instruction: What does の do here?
questions.note: の links one noun to another noun.

questions.instruction: To read a long sentence, what do you look for first?
questions.note: Find the final engine and its carriage, then attach each piece.
